theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: How does permanent hair colour work?
options: Small colour molecules go inside the hair and join into larger ones
It coats the outside of each hair and washes out after a few shampoos
It stains only the outer cuticle, so it fades away in about a week
It feeds colour into the root so that new hair grows out coloured

questions.stem: What does the developer do in a permanent colour mix?
options: It softens and conditions the hair so that it is easier to comb through
It gives the mixture its smell, so you can tell that it is working
It develops the colour inside the hair and lightens natural pigment
It keeps the colour from staining the client's skin and scalp

questions.stem: What is the job of the alkaline ingredient (such as ammonia) in permanent colour?
options: To give the colour a fresh, clean smell when it is mixed
To close the cuticle tightly and add shine to the finished hair
To swell the hair and open the cuticle so colour can enter
To stop the finished colour from fading in the hot sun

questions.stem: On the usual level system for hair colour, what does level 1 mean?
options: Black
Lightest blonde
Medium brown
Dark copper red

questions.stem: What does the 'tone' of a hair colour describe?
options: How dark or how light the colour is on a chart
How many weeks the colour will last on the hair
How much grey hair the colour will cover
Whether the colour looks warm, cool or neutral

questions.stem: Which colour is used to neutralise (cancel out) an unwanted orange tone?
options: Red
Yellow
Green
Blue

questions.stem: Which colour cancels out unwanted yellow (brassy) tones?
options: Violet
Orange
Red
Gold

questions.stem: Which three colours are the primary colours?
options: Red, green and orange
Red, yellow and blue
Violet, green and orange
Blue, green and gold

questions.stem: When very dark natural hair is lightened, which warm tones usually show first?
options: Blue and green
Ash and violet
Silver and grey
Red and orange

questions.stem: How should you find the client's natural base level?
options: Look at the ends of the hair under the salon's yellow light
Compare dry roots with the shade chart in good daylight
Ask the client what colour was on her last box of dye
Look at the colour of her eyebrows and eyelashes only

questions.stem: Why do you ask whether the client has used henna or home dyes?
options: Some can react badly with peroxide and damage the hair
Henna makes the permanent colour work twice as fast as usual
Home dyes make the skin test unnecessary
The salon must charge extra for removing home dye

questions.stem: Shanice's skin test for colour shows redness and swelling. What should you do?
options: Do not colour her hair, and advise her to see a doctor
Colour her hair, but leave the colour on for less time
Use a stronger developer so the colour works faster
Put barrier cream on her scalp and colour as planned

questions.stem: How is a skin test for permanent colour usually done?
options: Paint the colour on the client's whole hairline and rinse it after 5 minutes
Put a drop of developer on the back of the hand and wipe it off at once
Apply colour to a strand of hair and look at it after 30 minutes
Dab a little product on a small patch of clean skin, as the maker says

questions.stem: What does a strand test show before a full permanent colour?
options: Whether the client's skin is allergic to the colour
The colour result and timing on a small piece of hair
How fast the client's hair is growing each month
Whether the client will like the price of the service

questions.stem: In general, how does a higher-strength developer differ from a lower-strength one?
options: It lifts more, but is harsher on the hair and scalp
It gives a darker, richer result and is gentler on the hair
It makes the finished colour wash out after a shorter time
It is only used on grey hair when the hair is very fine

questions.stem: Ricardo wants to go one level darker, with no lift. What strength of developer does the maker usually advise for this?
options: The very strongest developer that the salon has in stock
A low-strength developer, as the maker's chart shows
No developer at all, just warm water mixed in
Two developers of different strengths mixed together

questions.stem: When should permanent colour and developer be mixed?
options: Just before use, in the amounts the maker says
The night before, so it is ready in the morning
In a large batch at the start of the week
In the bottle, then stored for the next client

questions.stem: Which bowl and brush should be used to mix and apply permanent colour?
options: A metal bowl and a dry paint brush from the hardware store
Any kitchen bowl and a toothbrush from home
A clean plastic or glass bowl and a tint brush
A metal bowl and the client's own hairbrush

questions.stem: Why should you measure the colour and developer carefully?
options: So that the mixed colour smells a lot less strong
Because the salon is charged for every gram it uses
To make the mixture thick enough to stay on the comb
Wrong amounts can change the result and the timing

questions.stem: Tanisha has never coloured her hair and wants to go two levels lighter. Where do you usually apply the colour first?
options: At the roots first, then pull it through to the ends
Only on the ends, and never on the roots
Mid-lengths and ends first, then the roots later
On the roots only, leaving the rest of the hair

questions.stem: Why do the roots go on last when colouring hair lighter for the first time?
options: The roots are the oldest hair, so they need less colour
Heat from the scalp makes the roots process faster
The roots are more porous than the ends of the hair
Colour on the roots would stain the skin too much

questions.stem: When doing a regrowth (root) retouch, where should the colour be applied?
options: To the whole length of the hair, every time
Only to the new growth, without overlapping
Only to the ends, which have faded the most
To the scalp, so that it soaks up to the roots

questions.stem: Why should a retouch not overlap onto hair that is already coloured?
options: It can cause dark bands and damage the hair
It makes the roots look lighter than the ends
It stops the colour from covering grey hair
It makes the colour fade faster on the roots

questions.stem: Why is the head usually divided into four sections before a colour application?
options: To work in order and apply the colour evenly
To make the colour on the hair process more slowly
To keep the client's head cool under the dryer
To use a lot less colour than the maker says

questions.stem: How thick should the sub-sections (thin slices of hair) be when applying colour?
options: About 5 cm thick, to save time on a busy day
As thick as the whole tint brush is long
Thin, so the colour covers every hair
Any size at all, as long as the hair is dry

questions.stem: Why can grey (white) hair be harder to colour?
options: It is always too porous, so the colour runs straight out
It grows faster than hair that has pigment
It has extra pigment that blocks the colour
Its cuticle is often tight, so colour takes longer to enter

questions.stem: Can permanent colour make hair lighter if it already has dark artificial colour on it?
options: Yes, any lighter shade will lift off the old colour
Yes, if it is left on for twice the maker's time
Yes, if a higher-strength developer is used
No, colour does not lift artificial colour

questions.stem: Petrina's hair is relaxed. Why does it need extra care when colouring?
options: Relaxed hair resists colour, so it needs the strongest developer
Relaxed hair can only be coloured jet black
Relaxed hair is often porous and fragile, so it can break
Relaxed hair needs no skin test before colour

questions.stem: When colouring natural coily hair, why are small sections and full saturation (covering every hair well) important?
options: Coily hair takes colour faster, so less product is needed
Small sections stop the colour from smelling strong
Coily hair should be coloured dry only at the ends
Tight coils are hard to cover, so colour can miss some hair

questions.stem: How long should permanent colour be left to process?
options: Until it starts to tingle on the scalp
For the full time the maker says
Always 10 minutes, whatever the shade
Until the colour in the bowl turns dark

questions.stem: Why should you not put the client under extra heat unless the maker says to?
options: Heat makes the colour fade away before it is rinsed off
Heat stops the colour from covering any grey hair at all
Heat speeds up processing and can harm the hair or scalp
Heat makes the skin test result change

questions.stem: At the end of processing, why do you add a little warm water and massage the colour before rinsing?
options: To lift stains off the hairline and loosen the colour
To make the colour process a little longer on the ends
To mix in more developer for a brighter result
To cool the scalp before applying the next colour

questions.stem: After rinsing out permanent colour, which products are usually used next?
options: A strong deep-cleansing shampoo and a clarifying rinse
A colour-care shampoo and an acid-balanced conditioner
A relaxer and a neutralising shampoo
A perm neutraliser and a setting lotion

questions.stem: Why must you wear gloves for the whole colour service, including rinsing?
options: So that the salon's sink and taps do not get stained
Colour can stain the skin and cause an allergy
Gloves help the colour on the hair to process much faster
Gloves keep the colour mixture warm while it is applied

questions.stem: Why should the colour area be well ventilated?
options: To dry the colour faster on the client's hair
To keep the developer cool and fresh in the bowl
To clear the strong fumes from the mixed colour
To stop the cape from sticking to the client

questions.stem: Mixed colour gets into a client's eye. What should you do?
options: Wipe it with a dry towel and then carry on with the service
Rinse it with a little conditioner to soothe and protect the eye
Rinse at once with plenty of clean water and get medical help
Ask her to keep the eye closed until the colour is rinsed

questions.stem: Why should developer (hydrogen peroxide) be stored closed, cool and out of sunlight?
options: So that it slowly turns into a thicker cream
Heat and light make it break down and lose strength
Sunlight turns it into permanent colour
So that it does not freeze solid in the store room

questions.stem: What should you do with mixed colour left in the bowl at the end of a service?
options: Cover it with foil and keep it for the next client
Pour it back into the tube to use another day
Put it in a sealed bottle and keep it on the shelf
Throw it away, as the maker and Centre's rules say

questions.stem: How should tint brushes and bowls be dealt with after use?
options: Rinsed quickly and left with colour on them
Washed clean, then disinfected and dried
Wiped with the client's used towel
Kept in the trolley drawer until the end of the week

questions.stem: What advice helps a client keep her new permanent colour looking good?
options: Wash it every day with a strong clarifying shampoo
Sit out in the hot sun often so that the colour sets
Swim in a chlorinated pool often to brighten the colour
Use colour-care products and protect it from strong sun

questions.stem: When will a client with permanent colour usually need a regrowth retouch?
options: When the new, uncoloured growth starts to show at the roots
Every week, to stop the coloured ends from fading out
Never, because permanent colour stays on the roots for ever
Only when the hair has grown long enough to reach the shoulders

questions.stem: Which details should go on the record card after a permanent colour?
options: The client's favourite music, drinks and magazines
Only the price paid and the date of the client's visit
Shade, developer, mixing amounts, timing and test results
The name of the colour the stylist likes best for herself

questions.stem: After a colour, there is colour stain on the client's skin at the hairline. What is the best way to remove it?
options: Scrub it off hard with a stiff nail brush and soap
Wipe it off with a little bleach on cotton wool
Leave it alone, because it will wash off in a day
Use a skin stain remover, as the maker says

questions.stem: Shauna-Kay's ends came out darker than her roots. What is the most likely cause?
options: The roots were coloured before the ends
Too little colour was used on the ends
The porous ends soaked up more colour
The developer was too old to work

questions.stem: During processing, the client says her scalp is itching and burning badly. What should you do first?
options: Tell her it is quite normal and leave the colour on
Put her under a hot dryer so that it finishes faster
Rinse it off at once and tell the instructor
Spray cool water on the colour to calm the scalp

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how permanent hair colour works inside the hair, and why it lasts until the hair grows out or is cut.
essays.modelAnswer: Permanent colour is mixed with a developer, which is hydrogen peroxide. The colour also has an alkaline ingredient, such as ammonia. The alkali swells the hair and opens the cuticle, which is the outer layer. Small colour molecules can then pass through the cuticle into the cortex, the middle layer. The developer does two jobs: it lightens some of the natural melanin, and it makes the small colour molecules join together into large ones. These large molecules are too big to wash back out through the cuticle, so they are trapped in the cortex. That is why the colour does not wash out. It stays in the hair that was coloured, but new hair grows from the scalp in the natural colour, so the client needs a regrowth retouch, and the colour stays on the lengths until it is cut off.
markingPoints: The alkaline ingredient swells the hair and opens the cuticle
Small colour molecules enter the cortex
The developer (hydrogen peroxide) lightens natural pigment
The developer joins the small molecules into large ones that are trapped
New growth is the natural colour, so retouches are needed; colour stays until cut

essays.stem: Describe a full consultation before a permanent colour service, including the tests you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: I sit with the client and ask what colour she wants, using the shade chart and pictures, and I make sure it suits her skin tone and lifestyle. I ask about past services such as relaxers, perms, henna, home dyes or bleach, and when they were done. I ask about allergies, any reaction to colour before, and medical conditions. I look at the scalp for cuts, sores, redness or infection, and if I find any, I do not colour and advise her to see a doctor. I check her natural level on dry roots in good daylight, how much grey she has, and the hair's texture, porosity and condition. I do a skin test as early as the maker says, often 48 hours before, and a strand test, and an incompatibility test if I think there is henna or metallic dye. I agree the shade, price and time, and write it all on the record card.
markingPoints: Agrees the colour wanted, using the shade chart
Asks about past chemical services, henna or home dye, allergies and health
Checks the scalp and does not colour (refers) if there is a problem
Finds the natural level, the amount of grey, and the hair's porosity and condition
Does the skin test (often 48 hours before) and a strand test as the maker says; records everything

essays.stem: Describe how to do a skin test for permanent colour, how to read the result, and what to do if it shows a reaction.
essays.modelAnswer: I follow the maker's instructions for the test. Usually it is done about 48 hours before the colour service. I choose a small patch of skin behind the ear or inside the elbow, and clean it gently. I put on gloves and apply a small amount of the product the maker says, then leave it to dry, uncovered. I tell the client not to wash or cover it, and to wash it off at once and call the salon if it itches, burns or swells. When she comes back, I look at the area in good light and ask how it felt. If there is no redness, swelling, itching or blistering, the test is clear and I can go ahead. If there is any of these, the test shows a reaction: I must not colour her hair, I write the result on her record card, and I advise her to see a doctor.
markingPoints: Follows the maker's instructions, usually about 48 hours before
Cleans a small patch behind the ear or inside the elbow and applies the product
Tells the client to leave it uncovered and to wash it off and call if it reacts
Reads the result: redness, swelling, itching or blisters means a reaction
If there is a reaction, does not colour, records it and refers to a doctor

essays.stem: Nordia has natural level 3 hair with brassy orange tones from an old colour. Explain how the level system and the colour wheel help you choose her new colour.
essays.modelAnswer: The level system tells us how light or dark hair is, from 1 for black to 10 for the lightest blonde. Nordia's natural hair is level 3, a dark brown. I check her roots and her ends against the shade chart, because the old colour on her ends may be a different level. The colour wheel shows that colours opposite each other cancel each other out. Blue is opposite orange, so to neutralise her brassy orange tones I would choose a shade with a cool, ash (blue-based) tone. If she wants a natural dark brown, I could choose a level 3 or 4 ash or neutral shade. I would also remember that colour does not lift artificial colour, so if her old colour is darker than she wants, tint will not lighten it. I would do a strand test to check the result before the full service.
markingPoints: Level system: 1 is black to 10 the lightest blonde; level 3 is dark brown
Checks roots and ends separately against the shade chart
Colour wheel: opposite colours cancel; blue cancels orange
Chooses an ash (cool) or neutral shade at a suitable level
Remembers colour does not lift colour, and does a strand test

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose the developer for a permanent colour. Describe the strengths in general terms.
essays.modelAnswer: Developer comes in different strengths, from low to high. A low-strength developer gives little or no lift. It is used when the client wants the same level, a darker shade, or a gentle grey blend, and it is kinder to fragile, relaxed or porous hair. A medium strength is often used for grey coverage and for small amounts of lift. A higher strength gives more lift, but it is harsher on the hair and the scalp and can cause more damage and irritation. To choose, I look at the client's natural level, the target level, the amount of grey, and the condition of her hair. Then I read the maker's chart, because each maker says which developer to use with each shade and how much to mix. I always use the developer from the same maker as the colour, measure it carefully, and do a strand test.
markingPoints: Low strength: little or no lift; same level, darker or fragile hair
Higher strength: more lift but harsher on the hair and scalp
Choice depends on the natural level, target level, grey and hair condition
Follows the maker's chart for strength and mixing amounts
Uses the same maker's developer, measures carefully, strand tests

essays.stem: Compare a first-time (virgin) application to go lighter with a regrowth retouch. Say where you apply first, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: In both services I gown the client, apply barrier cream, wear gloves and divide the dry hair into four sections, then work in thin sub-sections so that the colour covers well. For a first-time application to go lighter, I apply the colour to the mid-lengths and ends first, keeping it a little way from the scalp. I apply it to the roots last, because heat from the scalp makes the roots process faster. If I put it on the roots first, they would come out lighter and brighter than the rest, which is called hot roots. For a regrowth retouch, I apply the colour only to the new growth at the roots, without overlapping onto the hair that is already coloured. Overlapping can cause a dark band and damage the hair. If the ends have faded, I may take the colour through to the ends for the last few minutes, as the maker says.
markingPoints: Both: gown, barrier cream, gloves, four sections and thin sub-sections
Virgin lighter: mid-lengths and ends first, roots last
Reason: scalp heat makes roots process faster (hot roots)
Retouch: new growth only, with no overlap
Overlap causes banding or damage; pull through to faded ends only as the maker says

essays.stem: Describe the extra care needed when giving permanent colour to relaxed hair or to natural coily hair.
essays.modelAnswer: Relaxed hair has already had a strong chemical, so it is often more porous and weaker, especially on the ends. I check its condition and elasticity carefully, and I do a strand test. I leave the time between the relaxer and the colour that the maker says, and I do not do both on the same day unless the maker allows it. I usually choose a low-strength developer and a gentle shade, and I may use a protein or moisture treatment. Natural coily hair is often dry and can break when it is combed, and the tight coils can hide parts of the hair from the colour. I detangle it gently first, work in small sections, and make sure every hair is covered. I keep tension low and use a wide-tooth comb. After colour, both hair types need moisturising care, deep conditioning and gentle handling.
markingPoints: Relaxed hair is porous and weaker: checks condition and strand tests
Leaves the maker's time between relaxing and colouring
Chooses a low-strength developer or gentle shade for fragile hair
Coily hair: detangles gently, small sections, full coverage, low tension
Advises moisture, deep conditioning and gentle handling afterwards

essays.stem: Describe the safety steps for handling, mixing and storing permanent colour and developer, including ventilation, PPE and first aid.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the maker's instructions and follow them and the Centre's rules. I wear gloves and an apron, and protect the client with a cape, towel and barrier cream. I work in a well-ventilated area so that the fumes do not build up. I mix only what I need, just before use, in a plastic or glass bowl, and never mix products from different makers. I keep colour away from the eyes. If it gets in an eye, I rinse it at once with plenty of clean water and get medical help. If it gets on the skin, I rinse it off. If the client feels burning, I rinse the colour off straight away and tell the instructor. I store colour and developer closed, labelled, in a cool, dry place away from sunlight and heat, out of reach of children. I never keep mixed colour in a closed bottle, because it can burst.
markingPoints: Follows the maker's instructions and Centre rules; gloves, apron, cape, barrier cream
Good ventilation
Mixes just before use in a non-metal bowl; never mixes brands
First aid: rinse eyes or skin with plenty of clean water; get help; stop if burning
Stores closed, labelled, cool, dry and dark; never stores mixed colour

essays.stem: Describe the steps for removing permanent colour at the end of processing and finishing the service.
essays.modelAnswer: When the maker's time is up, I check the colour on a strand to make sure it has developed evenly and covered any grey. I take the client to the basin with her cape and towel still on, and I keep my gloves on. I add a little warm water and gently massage the colour at the hairline and through the hair. This is called emulsifying, and it helps to lift colour off the skin. Then I rinse with lukewarm water until the water runs clear. I shampoo gently with a colour-care shampoo and use an acid-balanced conditioner to close the cuticle and help the colour last. I remove any stains on the skin with a stain remover made for skin. I towel-dry, comb gently from the ends upwards, and style the hair. Last, I check the result with the client and fill in the record card.
markingPoints: Checks the colour is developed evenly when the maker's time is up
Emulsifies with a little warm water to lift colour from the skin
Rinses until the water runs clear, with gloves on
Shampoos with colour-care shampoo and uses an acid-balanced conditioner
Removes stains, finishes the hair, checks with the client and records

essays.stem: What aftercare advice would you give a client after permanent colour, and why must the details be recorded?
essays.modelAnswer: I would advise the client to use a shampoo and conditioner made for coloured hair, and to wait before the first shampoo for as long as the maker advises. Strong sun, sea water and pool chlorine fade colour, so she should cover her hair or use a protective product and rinse after swimming. She should limit heat styling and use a heat protectant when she does use heat. A weekly deep conditioner helps, especially on relaxed or natural textured hair. She should book a regrowth retouch when the new growth shows. The record card must show the date, the skin and strand test results, the shade, the developer strength, the mixing amounts, the timing and the result. This lets the next stylist repeat the colour exactly, avoid problems, and see at once if the client has ever had a reaction.
markingPoints: Colour-care shampoo and conditioner; wait before the first shampoo as the maker says
Protect from sun, sea and chlorine; limit heat; use heat protectant
Deep conditioning and a booked regrowth retouch
Records tests, shade, developer, mixing amounts, timing and result
Reasons: repeat the result, avoid problems, show any past reaction

practical1.title: Skin test, strand tests and a shade results chart on hair swatches
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare for a permanent colour service by testing. First, set up a safe colour station. Then each member carries out a skin test on another member who agrees to it, following the maker's instructions, and writes the date and time on a test record so that the result can be read when the maker says. Next, each member mixes and applies a different shade, or the same shade with a different developer strength, to labelled hair swatches. Use at least one natural dark swatch (level 2 to 4), one swatch with grey, and one textured or relaxed swatch. Time each swatch as the maker says, then rinse, dry and mount them on a results chart that shows the swatch before and after, the shade, the developer strength and the time. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Clean up and hand in the chart and test records once for the whole group.
materials: Permanent colour in at least three shades, with developers from the same maker in different strengths
Labelled hair swatches: dark natural, with grey, and textured or relaxed
Plastic or glass bowls, tint brushes, measuring jug or scales
Timer, card, tape and marker pens
photos: The colour station set up, with products, tools and PPE laid out
A skin test patch on the inner elbow, with its label (arm only)
Colour applied to the labelled swatches
The swatches after rinsing and drying
The area cleaned, products closed and stored
checklist: Wore gloves and an apron throughout and kept the area ventilated
Did a skin test as the maker says and filled in the record
Measured and mixed colour and developer in the right amounts, just before use
Applied colour evenly to the swatches and timed them correctly
Rinsed, dried and labelled the swatches clearly
Explained the result of one swatch using level, tone and developer strength
Threw away leftover mixed colour and cleaned, disinfected and stored tools and products
safety: Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules; never mix brands
Wear gloves; keep the area ventilated
Rinse at once with plenty of clean water if colour touches the eyes or skin
Do the skin test only on a member who agrees, and wash it off at once if it itches or burns

practical2.title: Permanent colour regrowth or full-head application on a model or practice head
practical2.brief: As a group, give a permanent colour service on a model who agrees to it, or on a practice head with human hair. A model must have a clear skin test, done as long before as the maker says (often 48 hours), and her scalp must be free of cuts and sores. The hair may be natural, textured or relaxed. Share the work: one member leads the consultation and finds the natural level; one gowns the client and applies barrier cream; one measures and mixes the colour; then the hair is divided into four sections and each member applies colour to one section in thin sub-sections, regrowth only or full head as agreed. One member times the processing. Members take turns to emulsify, rinse, shampoo, condition, dry and finish the hair, and give aftercare advice. Photograph each stage below, showing the hair only, never the face unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it. Hand in the record card once for the whole group.
materials: A model who agrees, or a practice head with human hair
Permanent colour and developer from the same maker, chosen for the client
Plastic or glass bowls, tint brushes, measuring jug or scales
Gloves, aprons, capes, towels and neck strips
Barrier cream, sectioning clips, tail comb and wide-tooth comb
Timer, colour-care shampoo and acid-balanced conditioner
Skin stain remover and client record card
photos: The record card with the skin test result (no names if the model prefers)
The hair in four sections with barrier cream on the hairline
Colour being applied in thin sub-sections
The full application finished, before processing
The hair after rinsing and conditioning
The finished, dried colour from the back and side
The work area cleaned and tools in the disinfectant
checklist: Checked the skin test result and the scalp before starting
Wore gloves and an apron, and protected the client's skin and clothes
Mixed the colour and developer as the maker says, just before use
Applied colour neatly in thin sub-sections, with no overlap on retouch
Timed processing as the maker says and checked the result
Emulsified, rinsed until clear, shampooed and conditioned correctly
Gave suitable aftercare advice and helped complete the record card
Cleaned up and threw away leftovers safely
safety: Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules; never mix brands
Do not colour if the skin test shows a reaction or the scalp has cuts or sores
Wear gloves; keep the area ventilated
Stop and rinse at once if the client feels burning, and tell the instructor
Rinse eyes or skin with plenty of clean water if colour touches them
